title: Candlelight reveals treasures in a long-sealed Egyptian tomb
dek: Howard Carter looked through a hole in a sealed door in the Valley of the Kings and saw a chamber filled with ancient objects.
body:
In the Valley of the Kings near Luxor, a team cleared the last rubble from a descending passage this afternoon and reached a second sealed doorway.

Howard Carter cut a small hole in the upper left corner and held a candle to the opening. Hot air made the flame flicker, but it stayed alight. Lord Carnarvon asked whether he could see anything. Carter answered that it was wonderful, then widened the hole so both could look by candle and electric torch.

The light fell on a crowded chamber of objects left undisturbed for more than three thousand years. Two dark statues of a king, worked in gold, stood among gilded animal-shaped couches, painted caskets, alabaster vessels, a throne and heaped chariot parts. The name of the pharaoh Tutankhamun appeared on many pieces, and another sealed door stood between the statues.

Lady Evelyn Herbert and Arthur Callender were present with the Egyptian foremen. Earlier seals had shown that the outer entrance was forced and repaired in antiquity, so an empty room had seemed possible. The first clear view eased that fear. The doorway was closed again and left under guard, with Egyptian officials expected for a formal opening.

The valley has been dug over for generations, and many believed little remained. Today’s glimpse suggests one royal burial was never fully stripped by robbers.

The notes made by candlelight that afternoon, and the objects that followed, still set a standard for recording an ancient site. An almost intact royal tomb remains one of the clearest views we have of the craft, belief and material life of pharaonic Egypt.
